newsitem.title: USA: Oil falters near post Gulf War highs.
newsitem.headline: Oil falters near post Gulf War highs.

text.p: Oil futures prices took a breather Tuesday depite more news of Mideast turmoil, but most traders doubted the rally was over.

Cocoa prices on the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange ended sharply higher on news the cocoa-rich Ivory Coast would not begin exports on Tuesday as expected while soybean values at the Chicago Board of Trade ended higher on reports China was interested in purchasing U.S. crops.
News of violence between rival Kurdish groups in nothern Iraq was enough to send the oil market sharply higher on Monday, but Tuesday traders essentially ignored the Kurdish news.

"The market's pulling over for a scenic break. It's certainly high enough to get a good view," said Peter Beutel, president of Cameron Hanover, a New York-area consultancy and brokerage services firm.

Crude oil for November delivery ended 20 cents a barrel lower at $25.42 on the New York Mercantile Exchange. Overnight, the price had set a post-Gulf War high of $25.72 on NYMEX's electronic trading system.
"I view today as a profit-taking day as opposed to aggressive new shorts coming into the market," said Gerald Samuels, a trader and managing director at ARB Oil.
"The factors that brought us up here have not gone away," Samuels said, referring to low heating oil stocks and growing global demand for oil products, particulary in Asia.
Heating oil for November delivery closed 1.00 cent lower at 73.07 cents a gallon, while gasoline for November delivery ended 0.62 cent lower at 67.08 cents a gallon.

Traders have generally viewed any violence in Iraq as a potential delay to implementation of the United Nations-Iraq oil-for-food deal, a scheme that would allow limited Iraqi oil sales for the first time in six years.
The Commodity Research Bureau's index of 17 commodities rose by 0.78 points to 246.27 on Tuesday, bolstered in part by a surge in cocoa and soybean futures.
CSCE cocoa prices ended the day sharply higher after the Ivory Coast, the world's leading cocoa producer, said it was delaying the official opening of its marketing season.
The exporting period was expected to begin Tuesday, but the starting date was pushed back because the government had not yet decided how much to pay farmers for the cocoa beans.
Cocoa for December delivery settled at $1,396 a metric ton, up $17 from the previous day.

Soybeans ended firm on rumours China overnight bought 50,000 tonnes of U.S. soybeans. China, traditionally a major buyer of U.S. soybeans, had been sidelined much of the year by soaring grain prices, but a $1.00 per bushel drop since July could prompt China to resume buying, market analysts speculated.
Soybeans for November delivery rose four cents a bushel to $6.92-1/2.
Still, traders were wary of prospects for a significant rally in soybeans because warm, dry weather allowed for rapid harvest progress in key U.S. Midwest growing regions.

The U.S. Agriculture Department on Tuesday said 40 percent of the U.S. soybean crop was harvested as of Sunday, up from 17 percent the previous week. Abundant soybean supplies could drown chances of a rebound.

"If the weather outlook is good they will probably beat it down again tomorrow," said Steve Bruce, an analyst with E.D. and F. Man International. "There is no reason for bulls to step up and buy. At best bulls will wait for the market to go sideways."
